title: Neurologic Diseases and Opportunistic Infections in HIV

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of fevers, headache, and gradually increasing confusion. The patient was known to have HIV and a history of nonadherence to her antiretroviral therapy. On physical exam, the patient appeared somnolent but had no focal neurologic deficits. A CT head and a lumbar puncture were performed. Investigations: Noncontrasted CT of the head: normal appearances CD4 count 85 cells/μL HIV viral load 450 copies/mL Serum cryptococcal antigen positive 1:128 Lumbar puncture: Opening pressure 32 mmHg CSF WBC count 4/mm3, CSF glucose 30 mg/dL (45–80) CSF total protein 110 mg/dL (20–40) CSF Gram stain negative CSF cryptococcal antigen positive 1:32
questions.lead_in: In addition to starting antifungal therapy, what therapeutic intervention is warranted?
questions.explanation: Serial lumbar punctures The patient has presented with cryptococcal meningitis and evidence of elevated intracranial pressures (ICP). Unlike some other causes of elevation in the ICP , pharmacologic management with either acetazolamide, dexamethasone, or mannitol is not effective in cryptococcal meningitis. The first-line treatment is serial large-volume lumbar punctures to reduce the elevated ICP . Neurosurgical interventions such as lumbar drain placement, ventriculostomy, or VP shunting are reserved for refractory cases or in patients with evidence of imminent herniation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q23

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man was brought in by ambulance after being found unconscious. His partner gave a collateral history of preceding symptoms for 3 weeks of fevers, headaches, and new-onset seizures. He was known to have HIV but had not been on antiretroviral therapy or taking antibiotic prophylaxis. The patient was originally from Brazil but immigrated to the United States 2 years ago. On physical exam, the patient was somnolent with rightsided upper and lower extremity weakness. Investigations: CD4 count 23 cells/μL HIV viral load 76,850 copies/mL Serum Toxoplasma IgG serologies negative CSF EBV PCR negative CSF VDRL negative MRI brain: 3 discrete hypodense masses in the cerebral cortex with contrast ring enhancement
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chagas brain abscess In patients from endemic regions, Trypanosoma cruzi can cause acute or reactivation disease, particularly in patients with advanced AIDS. The most common presentation is CNS reactivation leading to meningoencephalitis or brain abscesses, which presents very similarly to Toxoplasma with ring-enhancing lesions on MRI imaging. The negative serum Toxoplasma serologies and EBV PCR in the CSF make other causes such as toxoplasmic encephalitis or primary CNS lymphoma less likely while the patient’s country of origin in South America is endemic for Chagas disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q24

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presented with new-onset neurologic deficits. He reported having mental slowing, with poor concentration and memory loss. As an example, he reported getting lost when driving to his home of 20 years. He was known to have HIV and was taking antiretroviral therapy. Neurologic examination was normal. A CT head and lumbar puncture were performed. Investigations: CD4 count 760 cells/μL HIV viral load undetectable CT head without contrast: normal CSF white cell count 6 ×106/L CSF HIV viral load 12,588 copies/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most important diagnostic test to guide management?

options.text: B12, thyroid function, and syphilis screen
HIV genotyping of the CSF virus

questions.explanation: HIV genotyping of the CSF virus CNS viral escape syndrome is an uncommon condition that can be seen in patients with HIV on ART . It is defined by presence of CNS HIV replication in CSF despite viral suppression or low-grade viremia. New-onset neurocognitive symptoms may range from HIV-associated dementia to focal neurologic deficits. CSF pleocytosis is often present with a CD8 predominance. Clinical management should include assessment of the CSF genotype due to compartmentalized resistant virus that may be present in the CSF . If found, ART regimens should be changed based on CSF genotype results. A nerve conduction study would be used to evaluate for neuropathies. HIV-associated peripheral neuropathies are common in persons with advanced disease (CD4 cell counts <200 cells/ μL). They are usually distal symmetrical neuropathies. Several drugs may also be associated with development of peripheral neuropathies, particularly older protease inhibitors (i.e., indinavir, saquinavir, and ritonavir). This may also be caused by drugs used to treat opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining illnesses, like dapsone, vincristine, isoniazid, and ethambutol. Initiation of ART is recommended to reduce the risk of developing distal symmetric polyneuropathy, but it is unclear if it can reduce severity of already present disease. Symptomatic management with pharmacotherapy is recommended such as gabapentin and potentially secondline regimens like a tricyclic antidepressant and topical capsaicin. MRI are typically recommended to evaluate patients where HIV-associated dementia is a concern with severe deficits to rule out other common neurologic disorders like neoplasms or infections. Also, while MRI is typically included in the evaluation of a patient with neurocognitive decline and suppressed viral load, it would not guide management in this case. HIV-associated dementia almost exclusively is seen in persons who have not initiated ART with advanced disease (CD4 cell count <200 cells/ μL). Lumbar punctures may also be done when evaluating a patient with advanced disease and neurocognitive deficits to rule out other etiologies. However, CSF HIV RNA levels would not be diagnostic of HAD, and typically an elevated CSF protein and red blood cells may be seen. B12 deficiency, thyroid function, and syphilis should all be considered in a patient with dementia but are unlikely to have been undetected in a patient who has been under routine HIV care for a prolonged period.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of progressive right arm weakness and a 1-week history of increasing confusion and word-finding difficulties. He was known to have HIV , and although previously on ART he had been lost to clinical care and follow-up 3 years earlier. On physical exam, neurologic exam was notable for 3/5 strength in the right upper extremity and an expressive aphasia. Investigations: MRI of the brain: there are multiple discrete lesions in the cortical white matter and basal ganglia, which are hyperintense on the T2-weighted imaging sequences. CD4 count 125 cells/μL HIV viral load 45,200 copies/mL Serum RPR negative Serum cryptococcal antigen negative Toxoplasma IgG negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Antiretroviral therapy The most likely diagnosis given the clinical syndrome and characteristic findings on MRI of the brain is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by JC virus. The recommended treatment for PML is immediate initiation of ART to achieve immune reconstitution. Treatments such as cidofovir, cytarabine, and 5HT2a serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as mirtazapine have been tested but have shown no or inconclusive clinical benefit. The antivirals aciclovir and ganciclovir do not have activity against JC virus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q22

parts.text: 12. Name four indications to do an LP in a patient with HIV.

cohort_answer.text: Syphilis with focal neuro deficits/altered LOC; syphilis with failure to improve RPR dilutions as expected; HIV with neurocognitive concern/possible HIV dementia; cryptococcal meningitis with features of elevated ICP; failure of virologic suppression; intracranial abnormality on imaging; any concern for meningitis/encephalitis with altered LOC

questions.question: 18. A woman who has HIV (CD4 72) presents with seizure/focal neurologic deficits. CT head demonstrates 3 large grey matter lesions, largest ~3 cm. You suspect this is due to toxoplasmosis.

cohort_answer.text: 1st line: Pyrimethamine 200mg x1 dose then 75mg/day PO + Sulfadiazine 1.5g PO q6h + Folinic acid 25mg/day; alternative Septra 10mg/kg/day (TMP component) IV/PO divided q12h. If <60kg, Sulfadiazine dose 1g QID. Pregnant (16 weeks): Pyrimethamine 200mg x1 then 75mg/day PO + Sulfadiazine 1.5g PO q6h + Folinic acid 25mg/day; alternative Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin + Leucovorin. Alternative diagnosis: CNS lymphoma; also MTB, Cryptococcus.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman, who has never left Canada, presents to ED with fevers, confusion, and headache. She is found to have a CD4 count of 72 cells/mm3 and an MRI that shows 2-3 grey matter lesions. A clinical diagnosis of toxoplasmosis is made.

parts.text: What is the first line treatment for toxoplasmosis?
If this woman was 16 weeks pregnant, what would the first line treatment be?
What is the MOST likely alternative diagnosis, if not toxoplasmosis?

questions.model_answer: a) First-line treatment for toxoplasmic encephalitis: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin (folinic acid) for 6 weeks. b) At 16 weeks pregnant: pyrimethamine avoided if possible in first trimester due to teratogenicity, but for CNS disease (life-threatening) treatment should not be withheld - use pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-leucovorin beyond first trimester (16 weeks is second trimester, so standard regimen is appropriate); leucovorin mitigates pyrimethamine-related bone marrow suppression. c) Most likely alternative diagnosis: primary CNS lymphoma.

cohort_answer.text: Changes in memory, concentration, attention, motor skills common in HIV, without evident cause other than HIV, classified as HAND (ANI, MND, HAD). ART use decreased prevalence of severe deficits (HAD) but milder deficits remain common even with viral suppression. Risk factors: low nadir CD4, age, comorbidities (CV, metabolic). Dysfunction does not reverse with ART. Pathophys: early infection of CNS via trafficking lymphocytes, then autonomous infection of CNS monocytes/macrophages. Subtle sx: memory defects, slow thinking, trouble concentrating, apathy, social withdrawal, decreased coordination, altered writing, loss of balance/gait instability. Investigations: subtle EEG changes, CSF mild lymphopleocytosis/elevated protein, MRI greater subcortical than cortical atrophy, multiple hyperintense T2 lesions non-enhancing, no T1 intensity (distinguished from PML)

ART, although minimally effective in reversing HAND. In case of 'CNS viral escape' consider regimen with higher CSF penetration (PI based regimens associated with greater odds of CNS viral escape). Rule out other reversible etiologies and contributing factors. Non-pharmacological strategies

questions.question: 15 year old with HIV, poorly controlled off ARVs. Comes in with focal neurological signs and seizures, ring enhancing lesions. Had SJS to septra previously. Not on ppx.

parts.text: B) Treatment, when to stop secondary ppx

cohort_answer.text:
CNS toxoplasmosis
Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin (+leucovorin/folinic acid) x6 weeks then secondary suppression. Stop secondary ppx once CD4 >200 on ARVs for >3 months, no further signs/sx of toxo encephalopathy. Secondary ppx for septra allergy: Atovaquone

questions.question: A patient with HIV has white matter lesions with no mass effect. Fill in the table below: Pathogen/Cause | Associated Disease

parts.text: Fill in pathogen and associated disease for white matter lesions with no mass effect (4 entries)

cohort_answer.text: JC | PML. TB | TB encephalitis, tuberculoma. Crypto | Crypto encephalitis, cryptococcomas. Toxo | Toxo encephalitis, toxoplasmomas.

questions.question: 12. Name four indications to do an LP in a patient with HIV.

parts.text: Name four indications to do an LP in a patient with HIV.

cohort_answer.text: Syphilis (neurologic manifestations with positive serology; asymptomatic syphilis when CD4<350 and RPR>1:32; RPR not downtrending despite treatment). Cryptococcus (therapeutic tap to reduce CSF pressure; CD4<100 and screening serum CrAg positive). Suspected PML (JC virus PCR from LP). Suspected CNS lymphoma. Meningismus/Encephalitis (after CT, blood cultures, and antibiotics started per IDSA 2004 guidelines) - Cryptococcus, TB, CMV. Concern for CSF virologic escape. Toxoplasmosis - LP for T gondii PCR, cytology, culture, CrAg, MTB, EBV, JC virus (DHHS guidelines).

questions.question: 50yo M HIV positive patient with CD4 count 50copies/mL, non-compliant with ART presenting with ataxia and vague neuro symptoms, no headaches. No focal neuro symptoms on exam. No history of travel, lives in Toronto. No LP given. MRI brain shows diffuse multifocal lesions.

parts.text: Give 4 pathogens and their associated syndromes to explain the clinical presentation.

questions.model_answer: Four pathogens and associated syndromes explaining diffuse multifocal brain lesions with ataxia in advanced untreated HIV (CD4 <50): (1) JC virus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), causing multifocal, non-enhancing white matter lesions with subacute focal deficits, ataxia, and cognitive decline. (2) Toxoplasma gondii - toxoplasmic encephalitis, typically multiple ring-enhancing lesions with mass effect, though can present with ataxia/ill-defined symptoms if cerebellar involvement. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis, diffuse periventricular lesions, altered mental status, can cause ataxia and cranial nerve findings. (4) Primary CNS lymphoma (EBV-associated) - single or multiple enhancing mass lesions, can present with diffuse neurologic symptoms and ataxia depending on location.

questions.question: Gentleman with HIV has lived in Toronto his entire life. Noncompliant with ART and CD4 is 50. Presents with 3 weeks of altered LOC and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.

parts.text: What are the 4 most likely organisms and diseases they cause?

cohort_answer.text: PML - JC Virus; CMV; HSV; VZV; TB (possible to get hydrocephalus though). Other differentials more likely to have mass effect/increased ICP: Toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcal. Non-infectious ddx: CNS lymphoma (causes mass effect).

parts.text: Man from Toronto with HIV with CD4 50, 3 weeks worsening ataxia and difficulty concentrating and memory loss, probably other symptoms, no focal neuro though. MRI shows no space occupying lesions but does show multifocal white matter disease. What are four organisms implicated and the diseases they cause?

questions.model_answer: Four organisms and the diseases they cause in this HIV patient (CD4 50) with subacute encephalopathy and multifocal white matter disease without mass lesions: (1) JC virus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) (2) HIV itself - HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder/HIV encephalopathy (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis (4) Varicella-zoster virus - VZV vasculopathy/leukoencephalitis.
